top_stories.title: July CPI inflation report lands today — the week's key Fed catalyst
points: The July Consumer Price Index (CPI — the government's main gauge of what households pay for goods and services) is out at 8:30 a.m. ET.
Consensus looks for a 0.1% monthly rise and headline inflation cooling to 3.4% year over year.
A soft print would ease pressure on the Federal Reserve and, per Yahoo Finance, could rule out a September rate hike; a sticky print pushes bond yields up and pressures stock valuations.
Traders are split between 'sticky' (persistent) inflation that delays cuts and cooling prices that justify aggressive reductions, so S&P 500 and bond markets are unusually sensitive to a surprise.
A Producer Price Index (PPI — wholesale prices charged by producers) report follows Thursday.

unique_angles.point: Argues the report may pass without major volatility yet still reveal why interest rates are headed even higher.
Notes investors have been hedging (buying downside protection) into the release, with inflation still above the Fed's 2% target.

top_stories.title: AI earnings from CoreWeave and Super Micro revive the AI trade
points: CoreWeave (a cloud provider that rents out GPU computing power for AI) more than doubled quarterly revenue to $2.58 billion and disclosed a $104 billion revenue backlog.
CoreWeave added a fresh $21 billion Meta contract on top of an existing $14 billion commitment running through 2032; the stock jumped about 13% after hours.
Super Micro Computer surged on strong guidance, with both names riding AI data-center demand.
S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 futures rose 0.3% and 0.7% after two down days, as tech beats lifted sentiment.
Micron and TSMC echoed the message that demand for AI-related memory and chips remains astronomical; South Korean shares rallied on Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

unique_angles.point: About one-third of tech companies have raised full-year guidance and CoreWeave narrowed losses with 'expanding operating leverage' (profits improving faster than revenue), prompting the question of whether tech earnings ended the selloff.
Cautions the tech sector stays volatile despite the beats, reflecting doubts about valuations and growth sustainability.

top_stories.title: Strait of Hormuz standoff keeps oil traders guessing
points: Trump claims the US has 'total control' over the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint between Iran and Oman that carries roughly 20% of global oil shipments.
Iran says the strait stays closed until its conditions are met, while US Energy Secretary Wright claims Persian Gulf oil exports are near pre-war levels.
Oil prices wavered as traders doubted a near-term restoration of flows, with Washington–Tehran talks deadlocked.

top_stories.title: Data centers push into US neighborhoods
points: The share of US home sales within 5 miles of a large data center doubled since 2018 to 1.5% of 2024 sales, with no measurable hit to home values yet.
53% of Americans oppose nearby data center construction over electricity and water use, noise and aesthetics; New York, Texas and other states have enacted temporary moratoriums.
Wall Street Breakfast notes data center growth is also driving job creation and rising home values in tech-heavy counties.

top_stories.title: Market breadth widens beyond mega-cap tech
points: The equal-weight S&P 500 (which gives each company the same weight rather than sizing by market value) is outperforming the market-cap weighted index, showing gains spread across segments.
Investopedia flags sector rotation as tech retreats from highs and other sectors gain ground, raising the question of whether the market is structurally stronger.

items.title: New York City targets Amazon's subcontracting model
points: The Delivery Protection Act, from Council member Tiffany Cabán and backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, would force last-mile delivery operators to directly employ workers instead of using third-party subcontractors.
It creates a licensing system for warehouses and distribution facilities, sets minimum safety and training standards, and makes companies liable for worker protections at their own sites.
Amazon says it would have to relocate delivery operations outside the city; Amazon and allies spent over $5 million campaigning against the bill.
If passed it could be a template for other cities regulating Amazon, the second-largest US private employer, and would likely face legal challenges like NYC's blocked pied-à-terre tax.

items.title: Other corporate and policy moves
points: Oracle is planning another round of layoffs this month while spending billions on AI infrastructure.
Google's Gemini app passed 1 billion users as competition with ChatGPT intensifies.
The Pentagon opened the Golden Dome portal to broaden bids on the $185 billion program; Northrop unveiled its Raid Hunter air defense system and Lockheed pushed hypersonic missiles.
Senator Sanders called for freezing AI development; Oracle's Ellison threatened to pull Paramount out of California absent a settlement; CME will launch index-based hockey futures in September.

items.title: Consumer spending is cracking
points: Recent retail sales and consumer spending data came in unexpectedly weak, contradicting expectations of steady growth.
Consumption is about 70% of US economic activity, so slower spending typically foreshadows weaker corporate profits.
That clashes with still-resilient earnings reports, raising doubts about whether current profit margins are sustainable.

items.title: The S&P 500 is getting cheaper while setting records
points: The index has notched 26 record highs in 2026 even as its price-to-earnings multiple (share price divided by annual earnings per share) compressed by 7 points.

Earnings contributed 20.3 percentage points of the index's 14% total return — profit growth, not investors paying up, drove the gains, the reverse of 2023 when multiple expansion supplied three-quarters of returns.

items.title: Two mega-caps supply a third of all profit growth
points: Q2 profit growth is 50% across the S&P 500, the highest since 2021, but falls to 32% excluding Alphabet and Amazon.
Alphabet earned $9.11 per share versus a $2.88 estimate; Amazon earned $5.75 versus $1.82.
Neither stock has returned in proportion: Alphabet still lags the index and Amazon trails modestly.

items.title: Alphabet's capex binge dings the stock
points: Alphabet raised its 2026 capital spending forecast to as much as $205 billion and closed a $25 billion debt offering for AI data centers.
The stock fell 3% despite the earnings blowout.

items.title: Housing warning signs
points: A collapse in lumber futures preceded July's weak home sales, suggesting leading indicators are flagging cooling housing demand.

items.title: 'Chipflation' is reshaping enterprise IT budgets
points: A structural memory chip shortage could persist another two years, per JPMorgan, driving 'Fear of Missing Procurement' buying.
Companies are pulling forward PC, server and storage-array purchases to lock in prices ahead of further increases.
Morgan Stanley names HPE, Everpure and Lenovo as beneficiaries; price pressure is spreading to consumer electronics, with Apple and others raising prices.

items.title: Two-thirds of requested AI data-center power may be 'phantom'
points: Wood Mackenzie estimates utilities will commit to only 28% of the 1,066 gigawatts requested by data center developers — capacity equal to over 1,000 traditional nuclear reactors.
Developers' 'shotgun approach' to pitching projects inflates forecasts and complicates grid planning.
Cost overruns on grid infrastructure are typically passed to customers via higher utility bills.

items.title: Trump defends secret flight out of Turkey
points: The White House indicated Trump was aboard Air Force One while he was secretly flown out of Turkey last month on a different aircraft.
Trump said the Secret Service and military demanded the plan over unspecified safety threats, raising transparency questions.

items.title: Moderate wins Wisconsin governor primary
points: Moderate Democrat David Crowley upset Democratic Socialist Francesca Hong, signaling an ideological shift in the party.

items.title: Also in Bloomberg
points: A feature on how 'romantasy' publishing (romance-fantasy fiction) spawned a billion-dollar cottage economy.

items.title: Older workers are leaving the labor force
points: Participation among workers aged 55 and over is falling, pointing to earlier retirements or barriers to staying employed.
Near-retirees are taking radically different risk levels in their 401(k) retirement accounts, signaling uncertainty about readiness.
Household incomes for ages 45–54 vary widely, exposing gaps in retirement savings capacity.

sections.title: NYC Takes On Amazon's Subcontracting Model
points: 1. The Delivery Protection Act, introduced by Council member Tiffany Cabán and backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, would require last-mile delivery operators to directly employ workers rather than use third-party subcontractors.

2. The bill creates a licensing system for warehouses and distribution facilities, sets minimum safety and training standards, and holds companies responsible for worker protections at their own facilities.

3. Amazon says the legislation would force relocation of delivery operations outside New York City; the company and allies spent over $5 million on a campaign against the bill, while unions argue it's the blueprint for workers to fight back.

4. If passed, the measure could serve as a template for other cities and states to regulate Amazon, the second-largest private U.S. employer, and would likely face legal challenges similar to NYC's recently blocked pied-à-terre tax on high-value second homes.

sections.title: Infrastructure & Corporate Actions

2. Google's Gemini app exceeded 1 billion users as competition with ChatGPT and other AI assistants intensifies in the market.
3. Pentagon opened the Golden Dome portal to broaden contractor bids for an $185 billion program; Northrop unveiled Raid Hunter air defense system and Lockheed pushed hypersonic missile initiatives.
4. CME to debut index-based hockey futures in September; data center growth is driving job creation and home value increases in tech-heavy counties.
